en: You will set fire to my heart
And bring strife upon Beijing.
From time to time, in every age,
An enemy like you has risen within,
Destroyed my people,
And plunged into darkest night
The lofty honor I possessed.
So saying, Chyngtengir
Thundered like a lightning bolt.
When he saw Chyngtengir's wrath,
His brow twitched and his teeth ground;
How could he answer back?
His cunning tongue fell silent.
Though there was no rope or cord,
His hands and feet seemed helplessly bound.
Then, speaking softly but firmly,
Zhelzhetpes began his reply:
You are a warrior, mighty Chyngtengir;
You may cut off this wretched head.
But a people, its treasure, its homes—
You will gain nothing by acting so.
A khan's ambition is a maddened camel;
If it tramples you, it will finish you.
Yesterday, black-jowled Zulpukor—
You drew Zulpukor and brandished it;
Making men lick the sword's edge,
You scattered a thousand of us
And sent us against the white-capped people.
We watched them from without and judged them,
We ranged their land and examined it closely.
They too are sons of men.
Kenen is indeed a mighty hero,
And the army he has mustered stands ready.
Ala-Too is no land cheaply won;
Without spilling blood and waging strife,
Without splitting lungs in single combat,
He is not one to surrender his people.
His courage is no less than yours.
One young lad stands in his support,
The forty chiltens and holy Khizr are his true aid,
Ever present before his face.
He is one of the proven warriors,
A man endowed with sacred grace.
Two twin lions, two champions,
Alym and Kulansaryk,
Are lion-hearted sons he has.
However I look at him from every side,
Kenen is no son to be cheaply taken.
He is no foe you can seize as spoil
And make into your plaything;
His is no people of forty scattered tribes
That you may slaughter and butcher,
Nor am I there in his hands.
If you face them and level spears,
Blood will surely be spilled;
If you meet them man to man,
They will test the limits of your strength.
Use force, and they will fight.
The Kyrgyz warrior's father was a lion;
They strike fiercely and raise battle.
Those pass-ridden mountains are a hell;
A foe that splits lungs and severs heads—
Measured rightly, that is the Kyrgyz!
I have told you truly what I saw:
If you provoke war, you will slaughter them like sheep,
But if you stiffen in wrath,
You will only bring ruin on yourself.
That would be sheer folly;
Know this and take heed.
Thus Zhelzhetpes spoke,
Offering words as a warning,
Driving them home and speaking firmly:
My champion, listen to me.
When they heard this counsel,
The chiefs of the Kaldai said,
Are his words not reasonable?
If he rejects the mediator,
The khan's good fortune will depart;
The khan's strength will be broken.
If he torments the innocent,
The people's spirit will be corrupted.
What fault is there in this advice?
So Suradai asked him:
— Heed what the envoy says;
Without starting quarrel or strife,
Spare this one spoonful of blood.
This conduct of yours would be cruel,
O warrior lord and sovereign;
Restrain your seething anger.
Zhelzhetpes, who knows the nations—
Spare his spoonful of blood!
The robed men repeated it day after day,
The men of the stony lands spoke plainly,
The Kaldai and the common people spoke,
The entire multitude spoke,
And from Chyngtengir's hands,
From his encircling net of iron,
From his blood-shedding bullet,
From his burning red ember,
Zhelzhetpes, father of the people,
Was barely saved from death!
May God never show such a sight:
When the people are moving uphill,
In the season when horses grow black-tongued,
Would Lord Tengir remain unprovoked?
Without casting the world into strife,
Would Chyngtengir, your elder khan,
Will God strike him as he lies peacefully?
His whole mind turned to scheming;
The eighteen thousand worlds
Could not fill his belly by one hair.
I shall be sovereign of the world, he thought;
Leaving no one alive who makes the slightest move,
I shall slaughter and butcher them.
Those upon whom I loose my fury,
I shall neither kill outright nor let escape;
I shall flay the skin from their crowns.
To the forty khans' peoples of China,
To Manchu, Shibee, and Torgut,
To Solon and Kalmyk,
And to the Black Chinese tribes,
He sent word to muster troops.
They prepared stout horses to ride,
And chose garments to last ten years.
Misery boiled among the stricken peoples
As he issued a harsh command;
Ignoring every deficiency,
He began this vast calamity.
He had his wrestlers and warriors
Examined by his judges of men,
Made known to those with knowledge,
Measured with the closest care,
And appraised by keen-eyed judges.
When the fearsome musket cracked,
He chose the men who would not flee,
The champions who would not flinch,
Who would neither move nor stir,
Who, though doomsday's raging fire engulfed them,
Would not budge under hardship,
And would not sag beneath a load of stones;
Warriors who could drink and never sate on blood,
Who, once they charged, spared no life—
These he drove apart and selected.
The shallow-witted and fainthearted,
All those who bared their backs,
Those who rushed about in panic,
Who unsettled the people and ruined the realm,
And when grave trouble came
Trembled and fled—
He culled them with exacting care
And sent each to his proper place.
He wrought destruction beyond measure,
Choosing with hairbreadth care
One hundred souls from every thousand.
Chyngtengir gathered his army;
Over every thousand men
He appointed one worthy commander,
And over every hundred men
He placed a single captain.
There rose a clamor that split the earth,
An uproar that rent the sky;
He drew a myriad troops from his people,
Mustered solid as blue steel,
With great Mange at the army's rear
And great Zange upon its flank,
Men who held their people in their grasp;
Before them rode Lord Khan himself.
Regiment upon regiment,
They came pouring over the heights.
The mind reels and the tongue cannot tell it:
Swarming like grass upon the summer pasture,
They came surging forth,
Their instruments for cutting men
Chosen and carried with them;
So many Chinese came glittering forth
That the sun itself could not be seen.
They crossed vast reaches of land,
Fording rivers of running water,
Cutting through lofty, precious mountains,
Pressing onward without sparing themselves.
When they came out upon the uplands,
There at Bozdongul, the earth's midpoint,
They halted beside Bozdongul
And pitched their army's camp.
The tents went up and the host spread wide;
One cauldron for every ten men,
Their food was carefully apportioned.
The commanders of hundreds gathered,
The commanders of thousands made ready.
They raised mottled blue tents,
Shot maral deer on the cliffs,
And gave themselves to many pleasures.
The entire host settled into rest,
Sleeping propped upon their elbows,
Dozing briefly in repose,
Lying until their hips grew weary,
Reclining until sleep was sated.
Stars separated in the sky,
Pouring light upon the earth;
Overhead the stars began to scatter.
The dawn-sign Libra
Sped toward the qibla;
The whole dawn broke open,
And light poured upon the earth.
The cold wind before sunrise
Whistled down the valley;
Every living beast and creature
Stirred and raced across the ground.
The people woke and the camp grew restless,
Expecting an order from the commander;
The whole host stood waiting.
And there, behold Chyngtengir,
Clad in his robe of blue steel,
Raging like a blue-gray tiger.
Suurultai, resourceful in counsel,
Was an extraordinarily mighty khan,
And he had countless
Cunning judges of men.
Those who always traveled with him,
Those of surpassing wisdom,
Eloquent masters of speech—
He gathered many from the people.
The keen-eyed among them,
The sages who had seen much,
The judges who unraveled knots—
He roused them all together
And left none behind.
Men who would strike with an ax when challenged,
Men who could conceive far-reaching counsel,
The narrow men of wicked thought,
Craftsmen fit for every task,
Men who had cast aside weakness and proved their valor,
Steady, watchful champions—
Chyngtengir gathered them without exception,
Then raised his voice and began to speak,
Speaking quietly but with force:
Zhelzhetpes, who goes between the sides—
No soul can pass where Zhelzhetpes cannot.
Let Zhetpes go as the intermediary;
Let him carry word throughout the world.
Let him take six pack mules,
Let him take ample provisions,
Warriors who can drink and never sate on blood,
Who spare no life once battle begins.
Whose single head, if demanded,
Could be staked against a multitude—
Let him take such champion warriors beside him.
Let him travel the four corners
Of this round world in four circuits,
And through all five corners of the earth
Pass marking what he sees.
Let him find a mountain to strike,
Let him find an enemy to fight,
Let him find a man to face him.
Who dwell in Ala-Too,
Whose six forefathers were khans,
